nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What criteria were used to exclude studies during the full article screening?
nodes.answer: Studies were excluded if they did not report original research, did not use quantitative environmental assessment methodologies, or if the healthcare devices covered were not electronic.
nodes.paragraph: A total of 42 studies were selected for full article screening. During the full article screening, each study was assessed individually for relevance to the literature search theme. At this stage, studies were excluded if they did not report original research (i.e. literature review studies). We also excluded studies that did not use quantitative environmental assessment methodologies (i.e. LCA and footprint method). It is important to note that relevant studies mentioned in literature review studies had already been identified dur - ing the screening process and no additional studies were discovered. Also, studies were excluded if the healthcare devices covered were not electronic. The full-text screen- ing ultimately resulted in a selection of fourteen studies. Furthermore, the reference lists of the included articles were sought out to identify additional articles that fit within the scope of the research. After abstract and/or full-text screen- ing of the studies from the reference list, three studies were selected, resulting in a final total of 17 studies included in the analysis. The entire search strategy is depicted in Fig. 1. 2.3 Extraction of information and in depth analysis Extraction of information from the 17 selected studies was performed according to predetermined criteria.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is the significance of the planetary health framework in relation to radiology?
nodes.answer: The planetary health framework emphasizes that the health of humans and all living species is interconnected with the environment, demonstrating the need for sustainable radiological practices for overall health.
nodes.paragraph: Key Points Question What actions can professional societies take to improve the environmental sustainability of radiology? Findings Better understanding of resource usage in radiology is needed; action is required to address regional and global disparities in access to care which stand to be exacerbated by climate change. Clinical relevance Radiological societies need to advocate for urgent, impactful, and measurable changes to mitigate the environmental impact of radiological practice. Research and education, as well as adaptation and resilience to current landfuture climate and environmental threats, must be prioritized while simultaneously improving access to care. Keywords Climate change, Sustainability, Resource allocation, Radiology, Health services accessibility Graphical Abstract Recognizing the environmental impact of radiology and need for advocacy Sustaining a healthy planet is essential to human health, including individual, community, and global health [ 1]. The planetary health framework recognizes that thehealth of all living species, including humans, is inter-connected with non-living components in the naturalworld [ 2]. The environment in which we live directly impacts human health, including climate and weatherpatterns. Human activities, predominantly the burning of fossil fuels, increase greenhouse gases, driving anthro- pogenic climate change.

nodes.question: What was a significant finding regarding the existing indicators and their application?
nodes.answer: A general application linking ecosystem health and human health risks has not been established despite the development of several indicators.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The good functioning of aquatic ecosystems is essential for providing diverse ecosystem services that benefit humans. The degradation of ecosystem health due to continuous stress- ors, such as climate change or water pollution, is leading to an increase in human health risks and well-being. Indicators have been developed to determine human health risks from recreational and drinking water. Still, a general application to aquatic ecosystems linking ecosystem health and human health risks has not been done. We here reviewed indicators and indices applied to assess the health of aquatic ecosystems and their links with human health risk and well-being. We evaluated the extent to which indicators can witness a risk to human health and well-being. A total of 245 articles were reviewed, consisting of 185 on the assessment of aquatic ecosystem health and 60 linking ecosystem health and human health or well-being. Out of the 65 indices described, we evaluated the use of several parameters and their relevance to evaluate human health risks, including physico-chemi- cal parameters, bioindicators, contaminants, and pathogens, therefore covering the various sources of ecosystem disturbance. nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What types of indicators are mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The indicators mentioned are cross-sectoral indicators commonly reported on by different government departments such as health, treasury, education, labour, and environment.
nodes.paragraph: Similarly to those proposed by WEAII and Measuring What Matters, these indicators are cross-sectoral in that they include indicators commonly reported on by dif- ferent government departments (for example, health, treas- ury, education, labour and environment). While these indi- cators can all be considered important within an individual department and fall within their remit, some of our most intractable societal problems are cross-sectional in nature. These problems are likely to require cooperation across mul- tiple stakeholders to solve. Whilst the principles of a wellbe- ing economy are increasingly being embraced by policymak - ers, to our knowledge no study to date has sought to identify the preferences of the general public for the principles of a wellbeing economy as countries re-build following the dis- ruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. This study aimed to fill this gap in our current knowledge by assessing the relative importance to the Australian gen- eral public of the key principles of a wellbeing economy and to investigate the potential for heterogeneity in preferences in relation to these key principles between demographic subgroups. 2 Methods 2.1 Survey An online survey was developed and delivered to a sample of Australian adults (aged 18 years and above).
